Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 2.1 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 52400 (computed as 998 x 2.1 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.

Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.05x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.

Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.

Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 1.8 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 44900 (computed as 998 x 1.8 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.

Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -400 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 8.40x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.

Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 10 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 230 °C, 60 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.71 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.29 bar, activity loss 4% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.37 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.52 bar, activity loss 16% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.

Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% ethanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.9 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 14% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.2 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.

An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 14 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.

The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.019 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.541 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 71 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.

Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 197 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 0.9 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
